_meta.descricao: Catholic answers to classic objections about the faith and practice of the Church — confession, images, the intercession of the saints, the papacy, and more.
_meta.aviso: Presents the Catholic position in response to real and recurring objections, with respect for the Christian traditions that differ on each point — it does not claim to settle theological and ecumenical debates that remain open among serious scholars of different traditions.
_meta.revisao_editorial: Each entry seeks to state the objection in the most honest and recognizable way possible before answering it, avoiding the construction of 'straw men'.

itens.titulo: Why Confess Sins to a Priest and Not Directly to God?
itens.resumo: The Church teaches that Christ entrusted to the apostles the power to forgive sins in his name, not merely an interior piety without visible mediation. Auricular confession is the historical development of that authority, not a medieval invention.
itens.corpo:
The objection starts from a correct premise (God, and God alone, forgives sins) but concludes something that Scripture itself does not support in isolation: that this mediation must always be direct and without a visible human intermediary. The Gospels record Jesus saying to the apostles on the day of the Resurrection: "Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them" (Jn 20:22-23), a power to forgive concretely exercised by men, in the name of Christ, and not merely a general exhortation to interior conversion. The Church reads this passage as the foundation of the sacrament of Reconciliation: the priest does not replace God as the source of forgiveness, but acts as a visible sign, historically continuous since the apostles, of a reconciliation that also has an ecclesial dimension: sin wounds not only one's personal relationship with God, but also communion with the Church.

This foundation appears already in the earliest texts. The Didache, a work from the end of the first century or the beginning of the second, instructs the faithful to gather on the Lord's day and "confess your transgressions, so that your sacrifice may be pure" (Didache 14:1), linking confession to the celebration of the Eucharist. Scripture itself knows of confession before others: "confess your sins to one another" (Jas 5:16) and "many of those who had become believers came, confessing and divulging their practices" (Acts 19:18). The testimony is clear that reconciliation with God passed, from early on, through a visible mediation in the community.

The historical form of this mediation, however, changed considerably. In the first centuries a public penance predominated, severe and, as a rule, not repeatable: the grave sinner underwent a long period of canonical penance and was solemnly reconciled only once. The question became pressing in the crisis of the lapsi, the Christians who yielded during the persecution of Decius (250), handing over certificates of sacrifice (libelli). The Roman presbyter Novatian, elected antipope in 251 against Pope Cornelius, maintained that the Church could not readmit those who had fallen; Cornelius, supported by Saint Cyprian of Carthage, defended reconciliation after appropriate penance. The rigorist position was condemned, and the Church established the principle that no sin, however grave, lies outside the power of the keys.

From the sixth and seventh centuries onward, the so-called tariffed penance, introduced by Irish monks with their "penitential books," transformed the discipline into a private and repeatable rite, made to the priest and followed by immediate absolution. On this basis, the Fourth Lateran Council, convoked by Pope Innocent III and held in Rome in November 1215, prescribed in canon 21, Omnis utriusque sexus, that every one of the faithful who had reached the age of discretion should confess their sins to their own pastor "at least once a year" (saltem semel in anno), under penalty of excommunication, a disciplinary command that merely confirmed an already current practice, although it is sometimes cited, incorrectly, as its creation. In the era of the Reformation, the Council of Trent defined the doctrine in Session XIV, on November 25, 1551, teaching that Christ left priests "as presidents and judges" to whom mortal sins must be disclosed, so that they might pronounce, "by virtue of the supreme power of the keys," the sentence of forgiveness or retention. That the power to forgive is exercised by men was, moreover, already a cause of wonder for Saint John Chrysostom, who in On the Priesthood observes that priests "have received a power that God has given neither to angels nor to archangels."

In sum, the priest is not an obstacle between the sinner and God: he is the minister of a forgiveness that comes from God, the concrete sign that reconciliation with the Father is also reconciliation with the Church, the Body of Christ, and gives a visible guarantee, of divine institution, that sin has truly been forgiven.

itens.titulo: Isn't the veneration of images and saints a form of idolatry?
itens.resumo: The Church distinguishes "adoration" (to God alone) from "veneration" (of the saints) — the image is a visual reminder, not an object of worship in itself. The distinction was formalized at the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which ended the Byzantine iconoclast crisis.
itens.corpo:
The criticism usually cites the commandment against idolatry (Ex 20:4-5) as if the Church asked the faithful to worship statues and paintings — which the Church itself condemns. The theological distinction is precise, formulated already at the Second Council of Nicaea (787): "adoration" (latria), owed exclusively to God, is radically different from "veneration" (dulia), the honor given to the saints as models and intercessors, or from the special "hyperdulia" devoted to Mary. An image of a saint does not receive worship in itself — it is merely a visual aid to memory and devotion, in the same way that a photograph of a deceased loved one is not mistaken for the person himself, but helps us remember him and address him with affection.

This formulation was not born of calm reflection, but of one of the most violent crises in the history of the Church: the iconoclast controversy in the Byzantine Empire. Around 726, Emperor Leo III the Isaurian began a policy of destroying images, probably influenced by pressure from Islam, which forbade religious figures, and by motives of imperial authority. His son Constantine V (741-775) took the program to the extreme and in 754 convened the Council of Hieria, which condemned images and improperly presented itself as the seventh ecumenical council — without the presence of the patriarchs of the East or the legates of the pope. Leo IV followed the same line. After his death, his widow, Irene of Athens, acting as regent for their son Constantine VI, undertook the restoration of images, out of personal conviction and also out of political calculation.

The opposition to images had a weighty adversary on the Catholic side: Saint John of Damascus, a monk who lived under Muslim rule and was therefore beyond the emperor's reach. In his three Discourses in Defense of the Holy Images — condemned by the iconoclast Council of Hieria (754) after his death —, he argued that the Incarnation changed everything: if God became visible in Christ, it is legitimate to represent him. His formulation became famous: "I do not venerate matter, but the Creator of matter, who became matter for my sake." The discourses were decisive for the rehabilitation of the doctrine of images.

The first attempt at a restorative council, in Constantinople in 786, failed in the face of violence from iconoclast troops. The Second Council of Nicaea then met on September 24, 787, in the church of Hagia Sophia in Nicaea, with the participation of the papal legates (the archpriest Peter and the abbot Peter) and under the presidency of Patriarch Tarasius of Constantinople. In seven sessions, concluded on October 13, the council read the Scriptures and the Fathers (including passages that seemed contrary to images), examined the decisions of the iconoclast council, and approved the veneration of images, promulgating 22 canons. The letter of Pope Adrian I to the empress and the patriarch, read in the second session, attests to the consent of the See of Rome. The controversy would still have a second iconoclast outbreak beginning in 815, ended definitively in 843, in the episode known in the East as the "Triumph of Orthodoxy."

Therefore, when the Church says that a Catholic "venerates" an image, it does not authorize the worship that the first commandment forbids: the honor does not stop at the wood or the paint, but passes to the person represented, and ultimately to God. The image is an instrument of memory and affection, in the same sense in which Saint John of Damascus recalled that even the Cross, the book of the Gospels, and the matter of the sacraments are material things placed at the service of salvation.

itens.titulo: Why ask for the intercession of Mary and the saints instead of praying directly to God?
itens.resumo: Asking a saint for intercession is like asking a living friend for prayer: it adds to one's direct relationship with God and does not replace it. The "communion of saints" (from the Creed) teaches that death does not break the bonds of charity in the Body of Christ.
itens.corpo:
The practice is sometimes read as if it put Mary and the saints "in the place" of God, or as if it suggested that God needed intermediaries in order to hear a prayer. The Catholic logic is different: asking a saint to intercede for us is structurally the same as asking a living friend to pray for us; no one accuses that second practice of replacing personal prayer to God. The doctrine of the "communion of saints" (part of the Apostles' Creed) teaches that death does not break the bonds of charity and mutual intercession among the members of the Body of Christ; those who are already in the glory of God remain, in the Catholic faith, united in prayer with those who are still pilgrims in this life.

The doctrine that this clause summarizes rests on several biblical passages. In 2 Maccabees 12:43-46, Judas Maccabeus has an expiatory sacrifice offered for his fallen comrades, and the text concludes: "Therefore it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from their sins." In the Book of Revelation, the prayer of the saints in heaven is presented under the image of bowls of incense before the throne (Rev 5:8). The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the assembly of the "spirits of the just made perfect" (Heb 12:22-23), and Saint Paul compares the Church to a single body, in which each member contributes to the good of the others (1 Cor 12). It should be noted that the clause "communion of saints" does not appear in the longer ecumenical creeds (Nicene-Constantinopolitan), but in the Apostles' Creed, of Roman and catechetical origin; its oldest attested form appears in Nicetas of Remesiana (c. 335-414), a missionary bishop in the Danube region, who in his «Explanatio Symboli» understood it as the communion of "holy persons," the faithful, living and departed, united in one bond of hope and love.

The oldest testimony to this conviction appears in the third century. Origen maintained, explicitly relying on the communion of saints, that the Church in heaven assists the Church on earth with its prayers (On Prayer 31:5); Saint Cyprian of Carthage, in his letters from the time of the Decian persecution (mid-third century), writes of the Church as one body in which the martyrs and confessors remain united to the other faithful in charity. In the earliest period, it was devotion to the martyrs (the preservation of their relics and the annual celebration of their anniversaries at their tombs) that paved the way for confidence in their power of intercession. This evidence explains why the prayer of intercession is not a medieval innovation, but a practice attested from the earliest centuries.

The decisive doctrinal point is that the intercession of the saints does not compete with the mediation of Christ, but derives from it. The Second Vatican Council, in the dogmatic constitution Lumen Gentium (no. 49), teaches that the saints in heaven "do not cease to intercede with the Father for us" and "show forth the merits which they won on earth through the one mediator between God and men." The Catechism of the Catholic Church takes up this truth: the blessed "do not cease to intercede with the Father for us, as they proffer the merits they acquired on earth through the one mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus" (no. 956). The same holds for Mary: her maternal role "in no way obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ, but rather shows its efficacy" (no. 970); for this reason she is invoked as Advocate, Helper, and Mediatrix, without this meaning a second, independent mediation.

Thus, when a Catholic asks a saint to pray for him, he is not bypassing God or entrusting to a creature what belongs to God alone: he is exercising, with brothers and sisters already glorified, the same charity that leads him to ask a friend on earth for prayers, now enlarged by the certainty that those who are with Christ see God and intercede with greater efficacy.

itens.titulo: What Is the Biblical Foundation for the Primacy of the Pope?
itens.resumo: The Church grounds the Petrine primacy in Matthew 16:18-19 — the Kepha/Petros-petra wordplay and the handing over of the keys, with Isaiah 22:22 as background — understanding this authority as transmitted to the Bishops of Rome.
itens.corpo:
The most common objection is that the "papal primacy" would be a late institutional invention, with no direct basis in the New Testament. The Catholic reading rests centrally on Matthew 16:13-19, in the episode at Caesarea Philippi: to Peter, who confesses Jesus as "the Christ, the Son of the living God," Jesus replies: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church... I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven." This is language of authority and foundation, which distinguishes Peter from the other apostles, even though all of them also receive the power of "binding and loosing" (Mt 18:18). The handing over of the "keys" is not a loose metaphor: it refers back to Isaiah 22:22, in which the "key of the house of David" is conferred on Eliakim, steward of the royal palace, as a symbol of full authority and of access to the kingdom — an image that implies the existence of a permanent office (chief steward), not merely a personal charism.

The most debated exegetical point is the alleged distinction between the two Greek words in verse 18, 'petros' (the name given to Simon) and 'petra' ("on this rock"). Some objectors hold that 'petros' would mean a small, loose stone, and 'petra' a massive rock, so that the Church would be built not on Peter, but on Peter's faith or on Christ himself. Weighty Protestant commentators reject this distinction. John A. Broadus observes that it "is almost wholly confined to poetry" and "is not uniformly observed," recalling that the ordinary prose word for stone would be 'lit(h)os' (Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, 1886); R. T. France explains that the feminine form 'petra' had to be made masculine as 'petros' only to serve as a proper name for a man, and that "in Aramaic it would be even clearer, since the same form, 'kepha', would occur in both places" (The Gospel According to Matthew, 1985); and Craig Blomberg concludes that "the wordplay... only makes sense if Peter is the rock" (The New American Commentary: Matthew, 1992). The philological argument rests on the Aramaic substratum: Jesus spoke Aramaic, and in that language the two clauses would use the same term 'kepha', with no distinction of size — as even the Syriac Peshitta confirms, which does not differentiate the two words. Thus, the objection rarely holds up in first-century Koine Greek.

What is debated historically is not so much whether Peter had a prominent role — this is widely accepted even by non-Catholic scholars — but whether this role was transmitted institutionally, in a binding manner, to the bishops of Rome who succeeded him. Catholics and Orthodox differ regarding the scope of this authority, although both recognize a primacy of honor for the See of Rome. The Catholic Church formalized the doctrine in the Dogmatic Constitution «Pastor Aeternus», promulgated by the First Vatican Council on July 18, 1870, under Pius IX. The text is brief — four chapters, grouped around the institution, permanence and nature of the primacy — and defines centrally: the apostolic primacy conferred on Peter, the perpetuity of this primacy in the Roman pontiffs, the (jurisdictional) supremacy of the papal primacy, and the infallibility of the Pope when he speaks ex cathedra on matters of faith and morals, definitions that are "irreformable of themselves, and not by the consent of the Church."

The promulgation took place in an acute political and ecclesial context. The Papal States were collapsing in the face of Italian unification, and the Franco-Prussian War broke out precisely in those days; Pius IX would lose Rome itself in September 1870, and the council had to be suspended, never having been formally closed. The definition faced strong opposition: in a preliminary vote (July 13, 1870), with 601 present, there were 451 votes in favor, 88 against and 62 "with reservations"; about 56 bishops of the minority (among them Darboy of Paris, Dupanloup of Orléans, Rauscher of Vienna, Schwarzenberg of Prague and Joseph Strossmayer of Djakovo) left Rome so as not to appear in the solemn approval. In the final vote of July 18, there were 533 votes in favor and only 2 against (Bishops Edward Fitzgerald of Little Rock and Luigi Riccio of Sicily, who later submitted). The theologian Ignaz von Döllinger, who refused the definition, was excommunicated in 1871, giving rise to the schism of the so-called "Old Catholics." Since then, the clearest exercise of the infallibility defined in «Pastor Aeternus» was the definition of the Assumption of Mary by Pius XII in «Munificentissimus Deus» (1950), which expressly invoked the conditions established in 1870.

itens.titulo: Why does the Latin Church require celibacy of priests if the apostles were married?
itens.resumo: Priestly celibacy in the Latin Church is a historically consolidated ecclesiastical discipline, not a dogma — it does not apply in the same way in the Eastern Catholic Churches, nor to every ordination in the Latin Church.
itens.corpo:
It is true, and the Church herself acknowledges, that at least some of the apostles were married: Peter, who is mentioned in the Gospels as having a mother-in-law (Mk 1:30). The Catholic Church does not claim that celibacy is doctrinally required by the nature of the priesthood — it is an ecclesiastical discipline, theologically justified by the imitation of Christ's celibate self-gift and by complete availability for ministry (1 Cor 7:32-35). For this reason it does not apply in the same way in the Eastern Catholic Churches, which ordain married men to the presbyterate (although their bishops are chosen from among the celibates), nor does it rule out exceptions in the Latin Church itself, such as the ordination of married former Anglican clergy in certain cases.

The thesis that the Church "invented" celibacy in the Middle Ages is contradicted by ancient documentation. The Synod of Elvira, held in the Roman city of Iliberris (the present-day region of Granada, in Spain), is the first known Spanish council and the oldest preserved disciplinary source of the Hispanic Church. Its date is disputed among historians — proposals range from about 300-303 (Louis Duchesne, who places it before the persecution of Diocletian) to 305-306 (Hefele) and 309 (Mansi, Grégoire) — which suggests treating it as "c. 300-306". Nineteen bishops and 26 presbyters gathered, under the presidency of Felix of Acci (Guadix), with the renowned Hosius of Córdoba present; of its 81 canons, canon 33 determines that "bishops, presbyters, deacons and all other clerics with a position in the ministry are to abstain completely from their wives and not beget children," under penalty of expulsion from the clerical state. The historian Karl Joseph von Hefele considers it the oldest positive ecclesiastical ordinance on the celibacy of the clergy. The discipline was taken up again and reinforced by the councils of Carthage (c. 390) and by the Decretal Directa (385).

As for the Council of Nicaea (325), a frequent correction is in order: its canon 3 did not legislate on the marital continence of clerics, but only on the women with whom a cleric could cohabit (prohibiting the subintroducta, the woman who lived with him in a "spiritual marriage"). Since the fifth century, especially from the historian Socrates Scholasticus (Ecclesiastical History I, 11), a narrative has circulated that Bishop Paphnutius of Thebes prevented Nicaea from imposing mandatory continence on married clerics. Critical historiography — including the official study of the Congregation for the Clergy on celibacy in patristics and history — considers this story "a myth, without any historical foundation," and Pope Gregory VII had already condemned it at the Roman Synod of 1077 as a falsification of history; it was widely used by the opponents of the Gregorian reform.

The consolidation of the mandatory discipline in the West occurred progressively. The First Lateran Council (1123), in canon 7, turned into general law the prohibition against clerics cohabiting with wives. The Second Lateran Council (1139), in canon 7, reiterating the Council of Pisa (1135), took a decisive step by declaring that marriages contracted after ordination are not merely forbidden but nonexistent (matrimonium non esse censemus), making the marriage of those who had received sacred orders invalid. The Council of Trent (session XXIV, November 11, 1563, canon 9) declared anathema anyone who asserted that clerics in sacred orders (or regulars who have solemnly professed chastity) can contract a valid marriage, notwithstanding ecclesiastical law or the vow.

This discipline was reaffirmed in the twentieth century: the Second Vatican Council, in «Presbyterorum Ordinis» (no. 7), saw in celibacy a sign that proclaims the Kingdom; Paul VI, in the encyclical «Sacerdotalis Caelibatus» (June 24, 1967), examined the objections and confirmed its value, and the 1983 Code of Canon Law (canon 277) establishes that clerics are obliged to observe perfect and perpetual continence for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven. The Latin exceptions are explicit and restricted: the so-called "Pastoral Provision," granted by John Paul II in 1980 at the request of the bishops of the United States, allowed the ordination of married former Episcopalian clergy; and the apostolic constitution «Anglicanorum coetibus» (November 4, 2009) of Benedict XVI, creating personal ordinariates for Anglicans entering into full communion, provides that the Ordinary, "as a rule," admit only celibate men to the presbyterate, and may petition the Roman Pontiff, case by case, to admit married men as a derogation from canon 277 §1. In all these cases the Holy See insists that this is an exception in favor of specific persons, without any change to the discipline. It is, therefore, an ancient reality and not a merely medieval requirement, but it remains disciplinary in nature — modifiable by the authority of the Church — and not a matter of dogmatic faith.

itens.titulo: Does Purgatory Have a Biblical Basis, Given That the Term Does Not Literally Appear in Scripture?
itens.resumo: The word "purgatory" is not in the Bible, but the Church sees there the final purification of the saved and the efficacy of prayer for the dead (2 Macc 12:46), a doctrine formalized at Lyons II (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563).
itens.corpo:
It is true that the word "purgatory" does not literally occur in any book of the Bible — the term (from the Late Latin purgatorium, "place of purification") became established later, in the theological tradition of the West. This, however, does not set it apart from other central terms widely accepted among Christians, such as "Trinity" or "Incarnation," which also do not literally appear in the Bible, but express a content that the Church understands to be present in it. The biblical basis includes 2 Maccabees 12:43-46 — Judas Maccabeus has an expiatory sacrifice offered for his fallen companions, and the text concludes that "it is a holy and pious thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from their sins" —, a text that Catholics and Orthodox accept as canonical and most Protestant traditions do not, and passages such as 1 Corinthians 3:11-15, about a work that is saved "as through fire," as well as Matthew 12:32, which distinguishes forgiveness "in this age" from "the age to come." It is significant that the Almeida Bible itself, in a Protestant edition, acknowledges in a note that 1 Corinthians 3 historically founded the doctrine.

The practice of praying for the dead is attested long before any medieval definition. Tertullian, around 211, referred to prayer for the departed as an "apostolic ordinance"; Augustine prayed for the soul of his mother Monica (Confessions IX, 13) and dealt with expiatory punishments after death in «The City of God» (XXI, 24-26); Gregory the Great, in the «Dialogues» (Book IV, ch. 41), refers to a purifying fire that purges light faults before the Judgment. The doctrine was gradually systematized by the Magisterium. The Second Council of Lyons (1274), convened in the context of the attempt at reunion with the Greek Church, used the expression "purgatorial punishments." The Council of Florence — transferred from Ferrara to Florence on January 10, 1439 — approved on July 6, 1439 the bull of union «Laetentur Caeli», read by Cardinal Giuliano Cesarini in Latin and by Cardinal Bessarion in Greek, in which it is professed that the souls of those who die with light faults or temporal punishments "are purified after death and can be helped by the suffrages of the Church." The Council of Trent, in Session XXV (December 3-4, 1563), dealing with Purgatory, taught that the Catholic Church, "instructed by the Holy Spirit, drawing from the Sacred Scriptures and the ancient Tradition of the Fathers," believes that there is a Purgatory and that "the souls detained there are aided by the suffrages of the faithful, but chiefly by the acceptable sacrifice of the altar."

It is worth correcting a frequent error in polemics: the claim that Purgatory was "created" at Florence (1439) or at Trent is historically and doctrinally inaccurate, since there was already reference to purgatorial punishments at Lyons II (1274) and patristic testimony from the first centuries — these councils formalized a belief already practiced; they did not invent it. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (nos. 1030-1032) defines Purgatory as "a purification, so as to achieve the holiness necessary to enter the joy of heaven," which is "entirely different from the punishment of the damned": only those who die in God's grace and friendship, but still imperfectly purified, enter it, since "nothing unclean will enter" heaven (Rev 21:27).

The interpretation of the "fire" was deepened by Benedict XVI. In the encyclical «Spe Salvi» (2007, nos. 45-48), he takes up the hypothesis of "recent theologians" according to which "the fire which both burns and saves is Christ himself, the Judge and Savior." In this reading, Purgatory is not primarily a place of temporal torment, but the soul's transforming encounter with the purifying love of Christ: "the encounter with him is the decisive act of judgment. Before his gaze all falsehood melts away. This encounter with him, as it burns us, transforms and frees us, allowing us to become truly ourselves." In a catechesis on Saint Catherine of Genoa (1447-1510), author of the celebrated «Treatise on Purgatory», the same Pope summarized: "Purgatory is not an element of the bowels of the earth, it is not an external fire, but an internal fire." The doctrine is thus linked with the communion of saints: the Church pilgrim on earth can assist, by prayer and sacrifice, the brethren who are being purified, without this interrupting the union between those on earth and those who rest in the peace of Christ (CCC § 955).

itens.titulo: Why Does Mary Receive So Many Different Titles (Guadalupe, Fátima, Aparecida...) If She Is One Person?
itens.resumo: Marian titles do not indicate "different Marys," but aspects, apparitions, or places of devotion referring to the same and only Mary — and the Church distinguishes them from doctrinal titles, which call for caution.
itens.corpo:
The multiplicity of names may suggest to an outside observer a kind of Marian polytheism — several distinct "Marys" being venerated. Theologically, however, all the titles (Our Lady of Aparecida, of Fátima, of Guadalupe, of Mount Carmel, etc.) refer to the same and only mother of Jesus; the title merely indicates the place of the apparition, an aspect of her life or a virtue particularly highlighted, or the specific image under which a community venerates her — in a similar way to how one person may be called by different names depending on the context (mother, daughter, colleague) without ceasing to be one person.

This variety has a basis in the Magisterium itself. The Second Vatican Council, in the constitution Lumen Gentium (nos. 66-67), when dealing with the nature and foundation of the cult of Mary, states that "the various forms of piety toward the Mother of God, which the Church has approved within the limits of sound and orthodox doctrine, according to the conditions of time and place, and the nature and ingenuity of the faithful, ensure that while the Mother is honored, the Son, through whom all things have their being and in whom it has pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell, is rightly known, loved and glorified." The oldest and most fundamental title, from which all the others derive, is that of "Mother of God" (Theotokos, in Greek): the Council of Ephesus, in 431, defined that Mary is truly the Mother of God, against the position of Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, who preferred to speak only of "Mother of Christ." The doctrine was defended by Saint Cyril of Alexandria and remains the root of all Mariology.

The titles linked to apparitions are even more numerous and datable. Our Lady of Guadalupe goes back to the apparitions reported at Tepeyac (Mexico) in December 1531, to Juan Diego Cuauhtlatoatzin; her feast entered the General Roman Calendar on December 12, and the Virgin is invoked as Patroness of the Americas. Our Lady of Lourdes refers to the eighteen apparitions reported by Bernadette Soubirous in 1858, at the grotto of Massabielle, in southern France, recognized after an ecclesiastical investigation (1860). Our Lady of Fátima, to the apparitions of 1917 in Portugal. In Brazil, Our Lady of Aparecida originates in 1717, when three fishermen — Domingos Garcia, Felipe Pedroso, and João Alves — drew from the Paraíba do Sul River a broken image of Our Lady of the Conception, later gathered into a devotion that became national. As the case of Aparecida shows, even the title of a local apparition or devotion is always a variation of an older Marian title (in this case, the Immaculate Conception).

There is, however, an important distinction that the current text does not mention: not every popular title has the same status. Some, such as "Co-Redemptrix" and "Mediatrix of all graces," were the subject of a recent document of the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, the doctrinal note Mater Populi Fidelis (November 4, 2025), which considers them inopportune or of limits that do not facilitate the correct understanding of Mary's unique place — for she herself is the first redeemed and cannot be a "mediatrix" of the grace she herself first received. The Church, therefore, does not uncritically endorse every invocation: legitimate titles, whether approved or tolerated, are those that lead to Christ, the only Mediator, and never replace or equal him. This is what the same Lumen Gentium recalls when it says that true devotion "consists neither in sterile and transitory affection, nor in any vain credulity, but proceeds from true faith."

itens.titulo: If Baptism already forgives sins and makes me a child of God, why do I also need Confirmation?
itens.resumo: Confirmation does not repeat Baptism, but perfects and completes it, communicating a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit that is distinct from and complementary to baptismal grace, and sealing the Christian for witness.
itens.corpo:
The two sacraments have distinct and complementary effects, not redundant ones: Baptism wipes away original sin and brings the person into the life of grace and into the Church; Confirmation, without repeating this effect, communicates a specific strengthening of the Holy Spirit. The Catechism (no. 1285) places Confirmation, together with Baptism and the Eucharist, among the "sacraments of Christian initiation," whose unity must be safeguarded: its reception is necessary for the completion of baptismal grace, and through it the baptized "are more perfectly bound to the Church and are enriched with a special strength of the Holy Spirit. Hence they are, as true witnesses of Christ, more strictly obliged to spread and defend the faith by word and deed." No. 1303 details the effects: Confirmation roots us more deeply in the divine filiation; unites us more firmly to Christ; increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit in us; renders our bond with the Church more perfect; and "gives us a special strength of the Holy Spirit to spread and defend the faith" and "never to be ashamed of the Cross."

The biblical foundation for this distinct outpouring is found in the Acts of the Apostles. In Acts 8:14-17, the baptized of Samaria, although already baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, had not yet received the Holy Spirit: the apostles sent from Jerusalem "laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit." The Catechism (no. 1288) reads precisely this text, and the laying on of hands that "completes the grace of Baptism," as the root of Confirmation, and compares its effect to the outpouring granted to the apostles at Pentecost. It is in this sense that the catechetical tradition situates Confirmation as a special empowerment to bear witness and to live the faith with adult maturity, and not merely as the initial condition of child of God received in Baptism.

The essential rite of the sacrament is the anointing with holy chrism on the forehead (in the East also on other sense organs), with the laying on of the minister's hand and the words: "Accipe signaculum doni Spiritus Sancti — Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit," in the Roman rite, or, in the Byzantine rite, "The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit" (CCC 1320). The matter of the sacrament is the oil of chrism, consecrated by the bishop at the Chrism Mass on Holy Thursday. The original minister is the bishop (CCC 1312), which means that the celebration ordinarily reserved to the bishop manifests the bond of the confirmed with the Church.

Here we can explain a historical difference that often causes confusion. In the first centuries, Confirmation was generally a single celebration with Baptism, forming with it, in the expression of Saint Cyprian, a "double sacrament." With the multiplication of infant baptisms at any time of the year and the multiplication of rural parishes, which enlarged the dioceses, it became impossible for the bishop to be present at all baptismal celebrations. In the West, because the bishop was to be reserved the "completion" of Baptism, the two sacraments were separated in time; the East kept the two united, so that Confirmation is given by the priest who baptizes, but with the myron (chrism) consecrated by a bishop (CCC 1290-1291). This same history explains why, in the Latin rite, the sacrament is usually postponed until the "age of reason" and celebrated separately.

Hence the question "why do I need Confirmation if I have already been baptized?" starts from a mistaken assumption: that the sacraments are substitutes for one another. They are not competing stages, but phases of a single process of initiation. When Confirmation is celebrated separately from Baptism, its connection with Baptism is underlined by the renewal of baptismal promises; and its celebration within Mass manifests the unity of the three sacraments of Christian initiation (CCC 1298). The candidate who has reached the age of reason must profess the faith, be in the state of grace, have the intention of receiving the sacrament, and be prepared to assume the role of disciple and witness of Christ (CCC 1319). It is therefore not a matter of repeating the forgiveness of sins, but of receiving a new strength to live and defend, in adult life, what Baptism planted.

itens.titulo: If the Bible speaks of "brothers of Jesus," how does the Church hold that Mary remained ever-virgin?
itens.resumo: Hebrew and Aramaic had no separate word for "cousin" — "brother" also designated close relatives, a meaning that passed into the Greek of the Gospels, as confirmed by the identity of the "brothers" as sons of Mary of Clopas and the testimony of Hegesippus in the second century.
itens.corpo:
Passages such as Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 mention "brothers" and "sisters" of Jesus — James, Joseph, Judas and Simon among them. The objection assumes that these words can only mean biological children of Mary. But neither the Hebrew nor the Aramaic spoken in first-century Palestine had a separate word for "cousin": the term used for "brother" ("ach" in Hebrew) also covered cousins and close relatives, a meaning that passed into the Greek "adelphós" (plural "adelphoi") of the Gospels, written in a Semitic environment. The Old Testament itself confirms this broad usage: Lot is called Abraham's "brother" (Genesis 14:14), although he was his nephew.

The New Testament offers concrete clues of identity. Matthew 27:56 and Mark 15:40 identify "James and Joseph" — two of the supposed "brothers" of Jesus — as sons of a "Mary" who is called the "wife of Clopas" and their mother, and whom John 19:25 presents as a relative of the mother of Jesus, present at the foot of the cross. If the same woman is the mother of James and Joseph and is distinct from "Mary, the mother of Jesus," then those "brothers" were not sons of the Blessed Virgin Mary, but relatives. Here a decisive pre-Nicene testimony enters: Hegesippus, a second-century Palestinian writer, whose accounts have come down through Eusebius of Caesarea (Ecclesiastical History IV,22 and III,20), states that Simeon was the son of Clopas and a "second cousin of the Lord," and that Clopas (or Cleophas) was the brother of Joseph. There is also a technical controversy: James, "the brother of the Lord" (Galatians 1:19), is also called "son of Alphaeus" (Matthew 10:3); this is explained either because Alphaeus and Clopas would be the same person with two names — "Chalpai" pronounced in different ways — or because they are distinct persons, all of them being, in any case, cousins of Christ. To this is added the narrative argument: if Mary had had other children, Jesus would hardly have entrusted her to the care of John, the beloved disciple, at the foot of the cross (John 19:26-27).

The three classical positions raised by exegetes and Fathers on who these "brothers" were deserve to be distinguished. The thesis of Saint Jerome — the "brothers" were cousins, sons of Mary of Clopas and, according to the interpretation of De Viris Illustribus, of Joseph; that of Saint Epiphanius of Salamis, in his Panarion, who held that they were sons of Joseph from a previous marriage, of which Mary would be the second wife (Epiphanius calls Mary "ever-virgin" on more than sixteen occasions and thereby combats the "Antidicomarianites," who denied her postpartum virginity); and that of Helvidius, a minority view that was rejected, that they were natural children of Mary and Joseph. Origen of Alexandria (c. 185-254), in the wake of apocryphal writings such as the Protoevangelium of James (mid-second century), also held that the "brothers" were sons of Joseph from a previous marriage; Clement of Alexandria (c. 150-215) maintained the same in his Hypotyposes. The Church has never defined which of the first two explanations is the true one, and this does not affect the dogma.

This reading is not a late invention, and the controversy has a date and protagonists. Around 383, when Jerome and Helvidius were in Rome, in the time of Pope Damasus, Jerome wrote the treatise Against Helvidius specifically to answer those who — like the layman Helvidius, relying on Tertullian and Victorinus — maintained, on the basis of the "brothers and sisters of the Lord," that Mary had had other children. The treatise is divided into three propositions: Joseph was not Mary's husband in fact; the "brothers" of the Lord were his cousins, not true brothers; and virginity is superior to the married state. The Greek term "aeiparthenos" ("ever-virgin") was already in circulation as an expression of the faith: it appears in the second creed of Saint Epiphanius (374) and was solemnly taken up by the Second Council of Constantinople (553), which professes the Word "incarnate of the holy, glorious Mother of God and ever-Virgin Mary" (DS 422). At the Lateran Council of 649, under Pope Martin I, her virginity — "before, during and after childbirth" — was affirmed dogmatically, with an anathema on anyone who denied it. The Church, therefore, teaches the perpetual virginity of Mary on the joint basis of Scripture, Tradition and the testimony of the Fathers, and not against Scripture. It is significant that liturgical and patristic language itself has preserved the formula "ever-virgin," which sums up the faith of the Church and answers the objection directly.

itens.titulo: If Jesus condemned "vain repetitions" (Mt 6:7), why does the Church pray the Rosary, repeating the same prayer dozens of times?
itens.resumo: The Greek word Jesus uses in Mt 6:7 (battalogeō) condemns the mechanical, superstitious babbling of the pagans, not repetition itself — which Scripture and the liturgy itself already practiced.
itens.corpo:
In Matthew 6:7, Jesus' warning is often cited as a condemnation of repetitive prayer: "In praying, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their many words." The Greek text, however, uses a rare verb — battalogeō — which is a hapax legomenon, that is, it appears only once in the entire New Testament, which makes its exact meaning a matter of debate among exegetes. The central idea is that of babbling, stammering or multiplying meaningless words, in the style of the Gentiles who believed that the mere quantity of formulas would have the magical power to force the gods to answer. What is condemned is not repetition as such, but empty chatter and a superstitious trust in the quantity of words.

The internal proof lies in the context itself. Right afterward (Mt 6:9-13), Jesus teaches the Our Father, a brief and straightforward prayer, and the Old Testament already knew repeated prayer: Psalm 136 repeats the refrain "for his mercy endures forever" in all of its 26 verses, and Psalm 135 does the same in several verses. The Book of Revelation describes the heavenly beings repeating "Holy, Holy, Holy" without ceasing (Rev 4:8). The book of Ecclesiasticus (Sirach) 5:2-3, for its part, condemns "much speaking" in the same sense of a vain multiplication of words. The Jewish and Christian tradition never understood such refrains as the battology that Jesus reproves.

The Rosary has historical roots that are older and more complex than the pious narrative that attributes it to a single apparition. In the Middle Ages, monks recited the 150 Psalms; since most lay people were illiterate, the practice spread of substituting 150 Our Fathers for them, counted by means of beads or little stones — a custom present in several religions long before Christianity. Over time, the Our Father gave way to the Hail Mary (whose first half comes from Lk 1:28, 42), and the so-called "Marian psalter," the Psalter of the Virgin, of 150 Hail Marys, took shape. The connection with Saint Dominic de Guzmán (1170-1221), much repeated in papal documents, is considered by historians to be a pious tradition: according to it, in an apparition around 1208, Our Lady entrusted the Rosary to the founder of the Dominicans as a weapon against the Albigensian (Cathar) heresy, which denied the value of the material world and of the Incarnation.

The format known today was only fixed centuries later. It was the Dominican Alan de Rupe (1428-1475) who promoted the division into decades and the meditation on the mysteries. Pope Pius V, himself a Dominican, published on September 17, 1569 the bull Consueverunt Romani Pontifices, which fixed the essence of the current configuration of the Rosary, distinguishing its two essential elements — vocal prayer and mental prayer (meditation) — and confirming indults and indulgences granted by his predecessors. It was also Pius V who attributed to the recitation of the Rosary the Christian victory in the naval battle of Lepanto, on October 7, 1571, and instituted the feast that is celebrated today as Our Lady of the Rosary. In 2002, John Paul II added, in the apostolic letter Rosarium Virginis Mariae, the so-called luminous mysteries, raising the total to twenty.

Theologically, therefore, the Rosary is not the "vain repetition" condemned by Jesus. Each decade of Hail Marys accompanies the contemplation of an episode in the life of Christ (the "mysteries"), and the repetition functions as a rhythmic background that sustains this meditation — a structure analogous to ancient forms of repetitive contemplative prayer, such as the "Jesus Prayer" ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner") of Eastern Christian spirituality. The objection applies, at most, to the abuse of the Rosary prayed in a mechanical and distracted manner — which is precisely what the Church also reproves, and not to the use of repeated prayer in itself.

itens.titulo: If the Church preaches evangelical poverty, why does it have such rich basilicas and works of art?
itens.resumo: The Church distinguishes the personal poverty required of the clergy and of religious from the artistic heritage accumulated over centuries through donations, protected as cultural property and placed at the service of the liturgy and of charity.
itens.corpo:
The objection rests on a confusion between two distinct levels. Evangelical poverty is a personal virtue, required above all of the clergy and of religious, who must live with sobriety and without attachment to personal possessions; the Church's artistic and architectural heritage — basilicas, paintings, sculptures, liturgical objects — was accumulated over two millennia, largely through voluntary donations from the faithful, kings, nobles and patrons, with the explicit purpose of giving dignity to the worship of God, and not of enriching individuals. The Catechism addresses this point in explaining poverty "of heart" (nos. 2544-2547), which is not opposed to beauty dedicated to worship.

The Church's own law defines what temporal goods exist for. The 1983 Code of Canon Law, in canon 1254, establishes that the Church "by innate right, independently of civil power, can acquire, retain, administer, and alienate temporal goods" and lists as its proper purposes: "to order divine worship, to provide decent support for the clergy and other ministers, and to exercise works of the sacred apostolate and of charity, especially toward the needy". The heritage is therefore not an end in itself, but a means ordered to worship and charity — and the same Code (can. 1257) qualifies it as "ecclesiastical goods", belonging to public juridic persons of the Church, and not to individual clerics.

The numbers give the concrete scale of this collection. The core of the Vatican Museums goes back to 1506, when Pope Julius II acquired the sculptural group of the Laocoön and installed it in the old Court of the Statues, today the Octagonal Court; it was there that the first papal collection of classical sculpture was formed. The institution of a museum "in the modern sense, open to the public" and charged with safeguarding ancient works dates, however, from 1771, when Clement XIV acquired the Mattei and Fusconi collections and founded what would be called the Pio-Clementine Museum, later expanded by Pius VI. Today the complex holds about 70,000 works, of which approximately 20,000 are on display to the public, distributed across 54 galleries and 26 museums. According to the 2023 Global Attractions Attendance Report, they received about 6.7 million visitors, making them the second most visited museum complex in the world, behind only the Louvre. Ticket sales yield a significant annual revenue for the Holy See — estimated at about one hundred million dollars before the pandemic — resources used for the maintenance of the institution itself and for its work.

Besides generating revenue that goes back into the mission, this heritage is legally protected as cultural property. In many countries, civil laws of protection make it inalienable; the Church itself formally commits to preserving it and to facilitating public access. At the international level, the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict, signed at The Hague on 14 May 1954, obliges States to safeguard cultural property even in time of war. In Brazil, the Agreement between the Federative Republic of Brazil and the Holy See, signed on 13 November 2008 and promulgated by Decree No. 7,107 of 2010, addresses the question in its Article 6: it recognizes that the historical, artistic and cultural heritage of the Catholic Church and the documents of its archives and libraries "constitute a relevant part of the Brazilian cultural heritage" and obliges the parties to cooperate to safeguard it. Paragraph 1 adds that "the proper purpose of ecclesiastical goods (...) must be safeguarded by the Brazilian legal order, without prejudice to other purposes that may arise from their cultural nature", and paragraph 2 records the Church's commitment to "facilitate access to it for all who wish to know and study it". Ecclesiastical heritage is thus treated as a good of the community, not as the private fortune of clerics.

The teaching of the Council upholds the coherence between faith, science and culture in this area. The constitution Gaudium et Spes (no. 36) affirms the "rightful autonomy of earthly realities": created things have their own laws and values, which man discovers and organizes, and such autonomy "is perfectly legitimate". The same Council (no. 62) recommends distinguishing the deposit of faith from the way it is expressed, recognizing the value of human cultures — among them art — as expressions that the Church welcomes and promotes.

Finally, it is necessary to distinguish the heritage of the institution from the behavior of individuals. Historical cases of personal enrichment of clerics, of simony and of mismanagement are recognized by the Church herself as moral deviations and as objects of reform. The medieval response to this problem was the rise of the mendicant orders, Franciscans and Dominicans, who made voluntary poverty their charism. In the Modern Era, the Council of Trent (1545-1563) promulgated reform decrees on ecclesiastical benefices, the residence of bishops, the suitability of clerics and the creation of seminaries, combating the abuses that the Protestant Reformation had denounced. More recently, the financial reform of the Curia, in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, sought to subject Vatican finances to controls and transparency. These episodes are treated as deviations from the official teaching on poverty, not as its expression. The same holds for the inherited heritage: it does not belong to this or that prelate, but to the community of the faithful and, in many cases, to humanity as a cultural inheritance.

itens.titulo: Did the Church persecute Galileo Galilei just for defending that the Earth revolves around the Sun?
itens.resumo: The case involved scientific and personal factors — empirical proofs of the Earth's motion were lacking — and in 1992 John Paul II formally acknowledged the errors of the judges of the past.
itens.corpo:
The Galileo case (1564-1642) is more complex than a simple confrontation between "science" and "faith." In 1610, with The Starry Messenger, Galileo reported observations made with the telescope — the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, the relief of the Moon — that undermined the geocentric system of Aristotelian and Ptolemaic roots that was then dominant. On February 25, 1616, the Congregation of the Index condemned the Copernican doctrine, and Cardinal Robert Bellarmine warned Galileo not to hold it or teach it as true. Galileo continued to discuss it and, in 1632, published the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems — Ptolemaic and Copernican, a work written in Italian and in a popularizing form, in which the defender of geocentrism, Simplicio, is portrayed as a fool, which enraged many.

In 1633, the Holy Office tried him and condemned him for "vehement suspicion of heresy," for having held as true the doctrine of the Sun as the center of the world, against the decree of 1616. The sentence was house arrest — not death or torture, as the popular myth sometimes suggests —, served first in the palace of the Tuscan ambassador in Rome, then in the house of the Archbishop of Siena and, finally, in his villa at Arcetri, near Florence, where he remained until his death in 1642, having still completed the Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Concerning Two New Sciences, the foundation of modern physics. It is common to confuse his fate with that of Giordano Bruno (1548-1600), burned alive for heresy in 1600 — which does not apply to Galileo.

Although today we know that Galileo was right about the motion of the Earth, direct empirical proofs were lacking at the time. Stellar parallax — the change in a star's position over six months, which demonstrates the Earth's orbital motion — was only measured by Friedrich Bessel in 1838, with the star 61 Cygni; before that, there was even the accusation that its absence spoke against heliocentrism. The aberration of light was discovered by James Bradley around 1729, while trying to measure that very parallax. As for the Earth's rotation, the convincing demonstration came only in 1851, with Léon Foucault's pendulum in the Panthéon in Paris. Galileo's critics, therefore, had genuine scientific arguments, although now known to be mistaken, in addition to personal tensions aggravated by the polemical tone of his writings.

The rehabilitation was slow and institutional. In 1979, John Paul II expressed the wish that theologians, scholars and historians examine the case, and between May and June 1981 a study commission was created, which presented its conclusions only more than ten years later, through the voice of Cardinal Paul Poupard. On October 31, 1992, on the occasion of the 350th anniversary of Galileo's death, in a session of the Pontifical Academy of Sciences, John Paul II publicly acknowledged the errors of the judges. Poupard summarized that, at the time of the trial, "the theologians failed to grasp the profound non-literal meaning of Scripture when it describes the physical structure of the universe," improperly transposing into the realm of faith a question of factual observation. The Pope observed that, since the Enlightenment, the case has become "a kind of myth," in which "the image fabricated of the events was quite far removed from reality," used as a symbol of the Church's supposed rejection of science.

This acknowledgment is part of the teaching of the Second Vatican Council. Gaudium et Spes (no. 36) affirms the legitimate autonomy of earthly realities and deplores "certain attitudes of mind" of Christians who, by not recognizing this autonomy, "have given rise to conflict and controversy and have misled many into thinking that faith and science are incompatible" — a passage in which commentators identify precisely the reference to the Galileo case. The episode is thus one of the most cited examples of the Church's historical self-criticism: the theologians' error was not to defend the faith, but to confuse a question of astronomy with a question of doctrine.

itens.titulo: Is It True That the Church Forbade the People to Read the Bible in the Middle Ages?
itens.resumo: It was medieval monks who copied and preserved biblical manuscripts for centuries; the occasional restrictions on unauthorized translations (Toulouse 1229, Oxford 1408) never amounted to a general prohibition of Scripture.
itens.corpo:
The myth that the medieval Church "banned the Bible" oversimplifies a more complex picture. It was precisely the monks — in Benedictine monasteries and those of other orders — who copied by hand and preserved the biblical manuscripts throughout the entire Middle Ages, in a work of centuries without which a good part of these texts would not have survived to the age of printing. Far from hiding Scripture, the great cathedrals and monasteries displayed it in stained-glass windows and frescoes, sometimes called "the Bible of the poor." What the reformers of the sixteenth century had in mind was not a people deprived of the Bible, but the defense of a specific translation: no complete Bible in English existed before Wycliffe, and Luther himself, in 1538, complained that he had never seen a German Bible in his years as a monk — a claim that reflects his personal experience, not the facts of the circulation of the text in Europe.

The translation of the Bible into vernacular languages was, in fact, a common and ongoing phenomenon in medieval Europe, long before the Reformation. The Gothic version of Ulfilas dates back to the fourth century, and about a thousand manuscripts or fragments of medieval German translations have been preserved. The so-called Mentelin Bible, the first complete Bible printed in a vernacular language (not only in German), came off the presses of Johannes Mentelin in Strasbourg before June 27, 1466 — when Luther had not yet been born —, based on a medieval High German translation of the Vulgate made in the region of Nuremberg, and was reprinted at least thirteen times until 1518. In total, it is estimated that at least seventeen or eighteen complete Catholic editions of the Bible in German were in circulation, in addition to about ninety vernacular editions of the Gospels and Sunday readings and fourteen German psalters, before Luther published his own New Testament.

What did occur, in specific contexts, was the restriction of unauthorized vernacular translations, especially when associated with movements that the Church considered heretical. In the south of France, the Cathars (Albigensians) and the Waldensians read and interpreted the Bible on their own — the Waldensians in secret "conventicles" — to support their theses; for this reason the provincial Council of Toulouse, in 1229, convened by Bishop Folquet of Marseille, prohibited the use of vernacular translations by the laity, allowing only the Psalter, the Breviary, and the Hours of Our Lady. It was a local measure, of a provincial council, not an ecumenical one, and restricted to the province; the Council of Tarragona, in Catalonia (c. 1233-1234), also provincial, adopted similar measures in the context of the struggle against the Waldensians and Cathars. In the fourteenth century, John Wycliffe and the Lollards spread an English version tied to condemned theses, which led the Constitutions of Oxford, promulgated on January 14, 1408 by the Archbishop of Canterbury Thomas Arundel, to declare it "dangerous" to translate Scripture and to forbid new unauthorized translations into English under pain of major excommunication. The Council of Constance (1414-1418) condemned Wycliffe posthumously, ordering that his remains be exhumed and burned.

The Council of Trent took up the question in the sixteenth century, in a polemical context with the Reformation. In the decree of the Fourth Session (April 8, 1546), it declared the Latin Vulgate authentic and reserved to the Church the approval of editions and translations, in order to avoid doctrinally biased versions. The so-called Tridentine Index (1564), through its Fourth Rule, even required written permission from the bishop or the inquisitor for the reading of the Bible in the vernacular — a rule that, in practice, soon proved difficult to apply and was gradually relaxed. It was only with the Second Vatican Council that the Church explicitly reversed the tone: the dogmatic constitution Dei Verbum (November 18, 1965) affirms that "access to Sacred Scripture ought to be open wide to the Christian faithful" (no. 22) and asks for "correct and suitable" translations made from the original texts. In short, there were occasional and localized restrictions on unauthorized translations, never a general prohibition of Scripture — and the Church herself, in the twentieth century, began openly to encourage the reading of the Bible by all.

itens.titulo: Does the Catholic Church Reject the Protestant Principle of "Sola Scriptura"?
itens.resumo: Scripture itself, in 2 Thess 2:15, commands Christians to hold fast to the traditions handed on both by word of mouth and by letter — the biblical basis the Church uses against the sufficiency of the Bible alone.
itens.corpo:
The Protestant doctrine of "Sola Scriptura" — the Bible as the only infallible source of authority for Christian faith and practice — is presented by its defenders (above all in the Lutheran and Reformed traditions) as the criterion that would guarantee the purity of the Gospel, without fallible human intermediaries. The classic Reformed formulation is found in confessional documents such as the Westminster Confession of Faith (1647), whose chapter I, §6, states that the whole counsel of God "concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man's salvation, faith, and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture," and that nothing is to be added to it, "whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men." It should be noted that the same confession, in §3, excludes the deuterocanonical books from the canon, and in §4 states that the authority of Scripture "depends not upon the testimony of any man, or Church" but wholly upon God; and in §5 it admits that "the testimony of the Church" moves us to a high and reverent esteem of Scripture, although full persuasion comes from the inward work of the Holy Spirit. Lutheran theologians usually summarize the principle by saying that Scripture is the "norma normans," the rule that governs all other rules.

The Catholic Church answers, first of all, with Scripture itself. In 2 Thessalonians 2:15, Paul exhorts the faithful to "stand firm and hold to the traditions (in Greek, paradóseis) that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by letter" — explicitly placing oral preaching (Tradition) and the written letter (Scripture) on the same level of binding authority, without suggesting that only the latter would suffice. The same logic appears in 1 Corinthians 11:2 and in 2 Timothy 2:2, where the faith is entrusted to a living chain of transmission. The classic magisterial response came at the Council of Trent: in Session IV, of April 8, 1546, the decree on the canonical Scriptures declared that the truth of the Gospel is contained "in written books and in unwritten traditions" received from the Apostles, and that the Council accepts them "with an equal affection of piety and reverence," fixing the canon and declaring the ancient Latin Vulgate edition authentic; whoever knowingly rejected these traditions would be under anathema. It was the direct response to the Reformed principle.

There is also a decisive historical argument: the first Christians lived for decades before the canon of the New Testament was defined, and the very notion of a closed list arose within the life of the Church. The Muratorian Fragment, discovered by Ludovico Antonio Muratori in the Ambrosian Library in Milan and published in 1740 in the "Antiquitates Italicae Medii Aevi," is a Latin copy preserved in a codex of the 7th-8th centuries from the monastery of Bobbio, with 85 lines, and is the oldest known catalogue of the books of the New Testament; the original, probably Greek, is dated to around 170-200, since the author refers to the episcopate of Pius I of Rome (d. 157) as recent. The complete list of the 27 books appears clearly only in the 39th Festal Letter of Athanasius of Alexandria, of 367, and in later synodal enumerations, such as the Synod of Rome (382) under Pope Damasus I. The very decision about which books belonged to inspired Scripture was made by the Church on the basis of living apostolic Tradition — and not the other way around.

For the Catholic Church, therefore, Scripture and Tradition neither compete nor are two separate sources: they "form one sacred deposit of the word of God" (Dei Verbum, no. 10), both flowing from the same wellspring and handed on by the Apostles. The Catechism (nos. 80-83) and the Second Vatican Council insist that the authentic interpretation of the word of God, whether written or handed on, has been entrusted to the living Magisterium of the Church, which, however, "is not superior to the word of God, but is its servant" (Dei Verbum, no. 10). It is worth noting that even the Reformers did not dispense with the creeds and tradition as an interpretive context — the Westminster Confession itself acknowledges the role of the Church's testimony and of the inward illumination of the Spirit —; the Catholic dispute is not against the use of Tradition, but against the thesis that Scripture alone, detached from the living Tradition of the Church, is the only infallible criterion of faith.

itens.titulo: Is it biblical to baptize children who do not yet have personal awareness or faith?
itens.resumo: The Acts of the Apostles record the baptism of "whole households" — an expression that, in the ancient world, naturally included children of all ages — and the Fathers of the Church already bore witness to the practice in the second century, with the oldest documented controversy dating from 253.
itens.corpo:
Movements that practice only "believer's baptism" (older children or adults able to profess personal faith) point out that the New Testament associates baptism with a conscious response of faith and conversion. The Catholic Church responds that the New Testament also narrates the baptism of entire "houses" or "households" — that of Lydia (Acts 16:15), that of the jailer of Philippi (Acts 16:33), and that of Stephanas (1 Cor 1:16) — and that, in the first-century Greco-Roman world, the Greek term oikos (house) typically included children of all ages, which makes it quite probable, for the Catholic tradition, that children were among those baptized.

The historical testimony of the first centuries reinforces this reading. Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around 189, states that Christ "came to save all through himself: all, I say, who through him are reborn in God — infants, children, boys, young men, and old men" (Against Heresies II, 22, 4). The Apostolic Tradition, attributed to Hippolytus of Rome (c. 215), prescribes: "Baptize first the children; and if they can speak for themselves, let them do so; otherwise, let their parents or other relatives speak for them" (21, 4), confirming that sponsors already answered on behalf of the person being baptized. Origen, around 248, declares that "the Church received from the Apostles the tradition of giving baptism even to infants" (Commentary on Romans 5, 9), and that baptism is conferred on infants "according to the custom of the Church" (Homilies on Leviticus 8, 3).

The first direct and explicit testimony, however, comes from someone who argued against the practice: Tertullian, in On Baptism (c. 198-200), acknowledges infant baptism as an established custom but advises delaying it, especially in the case of small children, given the severity of post-baptismal penance at the time — a clear sign that the practice already existed and needed to be challenged. Shortly afterward comes the most revealing episode: around 253, the priest Fidus, reading that Jewish circumcision was performed on the eighth day, began to postpone the baptism of newborns until that time. Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, then convened a council of sixty-six bishops of North Africa (letter 64), which rejected the proposal: no one agreed with the postponement, "on the contrary, we all judge that the mercy and grace of God is to be denied to no human being born" — it being impossible to wait even for the second or third day. The question under debate, therefore, was not whether infants should be baptized — that was already an undisputed practice, held to be apostolic — but only when. In the East, Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, in his Oration 40 on baptism (c. 381), shows pastoral diversity: in case of danger of death the child must be baptized immediately, but otherwise he recommended waiting until about the age of three, when the child could already hear and answer something; even so, he maintained that infants are baptized "by virtue of the faith of their parents." Saint Augustine (5th century) would sum up the faith of the Church: the custom of baptizing children "is not to be scorned" nor considered something that does not come from the Apostles (The Literal Meaning of Genesis 10, 23). Archaeology corroborates this: Christian funerary inscriptions, especially in the Roman catacombs (such as one in the Catacomb of Priscilla and another in the Catacomb of Callixtus dated 268, which records a child who "received grace"), attest to the practice as already well established in the third century.

Theologically, the Catechism explains that Baptism is not first a human response, but a free gift of God that precedes any merit (no. 1252). Just as children are born into a family and a culture before they can choose them, the Church understands that they can also be born, through the faith of the parents and godparents who commit to raising them in the faith, into the life of grace, leaving for the appropriate age the personal confirmation of this received faith — an itinerary later completed by Confirmation and the Eucharist. It should be noted that the doctrine recognizes that infant baptism requires, in order to bear fruit, subsequent education in the faith, and that the ancient practice itself presupposed that parents and godparents professed the Creed on behalf of the child.

itens.titulo: When Jesus says "this is my body," was he speaking only symbolically?
itens.resumo: In John 6, faced with scandalized disciples who walked away, Jesus does not soften his claim: he changes the verb to "gnaw" and repeats that his flesh is "true food" — language that the first Christians understood as real presence.
itens.corpo:
Many Christian traditions read the words of institution of the Eucharist ("this is my body") and the Bread of Life discourse (John 6) as symbolic language, similar to when Jesus says "I am the door" or "I am the vine." The Catholic Church points to a detail often cited in this debate: unlike Jesus' other metaphors, when the listeners in John 6 are scandalized and begin to abandon him — "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" (Jn 6:52) — Jesus neither backs down nor softens the claim to correct a misunderstanding, as he did on other occasions (cf. Jn 3:3-5; 4:32-34); on the contrary, he reinforces it: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink" (Jn 6:55), and he lets many disciples walk away for good (Jn 6:66).

A philological argument is usually invoked in this reading. In the Greek text, up to John 6:53 the verb for "eat" is the ordinary ἐσθίω (esthíō) or φάγω (phagō, "to eat"); from John 6:54 on, John begins to use τρώγω (trōgō), a verb that describes a more concrete and physical act — "to gnaw, to chew, to munch." The evangelist, who had already used the ordinary verb when he could have kept the metaphor, would thus have deliberately intensified the materiality of the statement, at a point when his readers were already reacting with scandal. It is prudent, however, not to overstate the argument: good Catholic authors observe that τρώγω does not by itself prove the Eucharistic interpretation — the weight lies in the discourse as a whole and in the reaction of the listeners. In any case, if Jesus were speaking only figuratively, it is hard to explain why he would not have clarified things for them when the crowd began to leave.

The Church reads this episode, together with the nearly identical words of the institution of the Eucharist in the Synoptic Gospels (Mt 26:26-28; Mk 14:22-24; Lk 22:19-20) and in 1 Corinthians 11:23-25, as the foundation for the doctrine of the real presence: under the species of bread and wine, after the consecration, the Body and Blood of Christ are truly, really, and substantially present, and not merely a symbol or a spiritual remembrance of his person. The doctrine was dogmatically defined under the name of transubstantiation by the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) and reaffirmed by the Council of Trent in its thirteenth session (1551), in response to the Reformers' denial.

The argument is not a late innovation. Already in the early second century, Saint Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–c. 107) warned against the heterodox who "abstain from the Eucharist and from prayer because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, the flesh which suffered for our sins and which the Father, in his goodness, raised up" (Letter to the Smyrnaeans 6:2). Around the year 155, Saint Justin Martyr wrote that "we do not receive these things as common bread or common drink; but just as Jesus Christ our Savior, made flesh by the Word of God, had flesh and blood for our salvation, so we have been taught that the food blessed by the prayer of his word [...] is the flesh and blood of that Jesus who was made flesh" (First Apology 66). About a century later, Saint Cyril of Jerusalem insisted in his mystagogical catecheses that the bread and wine truly become the Body and Blood of Christ.

A contemporary fact shows how relevant the question remains: a Pew Research Center survey released in August 2019 indicated that only 31% of American Catholics affirmed that the bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ, while 69% regarded them as "symbols." The result — disputed by later surveys with different wording (around 50%) — was described by Bishop Robert Barron as "a wake-up call" and prompted the creation of the National Eucharistic Revival in the United States (2022-2025). The episode illustrates why the debate over John 6 remains relevant: in it the Church sees not merely a figure of speech, but the biblical foundation of a doctrine attested since the first Christian centuries.
