itens.titulo: Is salvation received by faith alone, or are works also necessary?
itens.resumo: The Letter of James states that "a man is justified by works and not by faith alone"; the Council of Trent defined, in 1547, that good works not only manifest but increase the justice received. In 1999, Catholics and Lutherans jointly declared a consensus on the basic truths of justification.
itens.corpo:
The principle of "sola fide" — justification obtained exclusively by faith, without any contribution from works — is one of the pillars of classical Protestant theology, based above all on Pauline texts such as Romans 3:28. The Catholic Church does not deny the centrality of faith or the gratuitous character of grace, but points out that Scripture itself contains a direct counterpoint that is difficult to reconcile with the strictest reading of "sola fide": the Letter of James states, almost as a response to this formulation, that "a man is justified by works and not by faith alone" (Jas 2:24), adding that "faith without works is dead" (Jas 2:26).

The Catholic reading seeks to harmonize Paul and James, not to set them against each other: the faith that saves is not mere intellectual assent, but living faith, "working through charity" (Gal 5:6), and it is this active charity that necessarily translates into works. Works do not "buy" salvation nor do they precede grace — which is always a gratuitous gift of God — but they are the necessary fruit and visible expression of a truly living faith. It should also be noted that James cites precisely the case of Abraham (Jas 2:21-23), the same example Paul uses in Romans 4 — a sign that the apparent divergence between the two apostles is resolved in the way the term "to justify" is understood: to declare righteous the ungodly person who believes (Paul), or to demonstrate the righteousness already received through works of faith (James).

It was exactly this question that the Council of Trent wished to define. Convened after the Reformation, the council promulgated, on January 13, 1547 (sixth session, under Pope Paul III), the Decree on Justification — the longest doctrinal decree of the Tridentine corpus: a proem, sixteen chapters of positive teaching and thirty-three canons with explicit anathema. It responds directly to the Reformed positions that had been circulating since the Augsburg Confession (1530) and the first writings of Calvin. The session affirms that faith is "the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of all justification, without which it is impossible to please God" (ch. 8), but that one is not justified "by faith alone," and that the justice received is preserved and also increased before God by good works (cf. can. 24).

For this reason Trent distinguishes two moments: initial justification (the work of grace, received in Baptism through faith) and growth in justice, in which the faithful, with God's grace, "cooperate" — the decree speaks of "increasing" in justice and of "faith cooperating with good works" (ch. 10). Canon 9 condemns anyone who says that the ungodly is justified "by faith alone" ("let him be anathema"), and canon 24 condemns anyone who denies that good works preserve and increase justice, treating them as mere "fruits and signs." The Catholic formula, therefore, rejects both salvation "by works" without grace (can. 1) and the reduction of justification to a purely external act of declaration, and situates works within the life of grace: not as the cause of salvation, but as a cooperating response to it.

It is worth recording the later ecumenical development. On October 31, 1999, in Augsburg, the Lutheran bishop Christian Krause, then president of the Lutheran World Federation, and Cardinal Edward I. Cassidy, representing the Holy See, signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification. The document maintains that Catholics and Lutherans profess the same basic understanding of justification by grace through faith, albeit with different emphases and developments; its no. 41 states that the doctrinal condemnations of the sixteenth century, "insofar as they relate to the doctrine of justification," do not apply to the doctrine set forth in the Declaration, and vice versa. The Declaration was later endorsed by the World Methodist Council (2006), the Anglican Communion (2017) and the World Communion of Reformed Churches (2017), but was rejected by more conservative Lutherans, such as the Missouri Synod and, in 2015, the International Lutheran Council. The Catholic Church, for its part, accompanied it with an official Response in which it acknowledges the progress without considering it a consensus that eliminates every remaining difference.

itens.titulo: Is there a real historical continuity between the Apostles and the papacy of today, or is it a late construction?
itens.resumo: As early as the end of the first century, Clement of Rome spoke of an orderly succession from the Apostles; and, around the year 180, Irenaeus of Lyon listed by name the bishops of Rome from Peter to Eleutherius, his contemporary.
itens.corpo:
The objection usually assumes that the structure of bishops succeeding the Apostles, with a prominent role for the bishop of Rome, was only consolidated centuries later, for political reasons. The oldest testimonies, however, place this awareness very early. The oldest Christian document outside the New Testament to address the subject is the First Letter of Clement to the Corinthians (c. 80-96), written by the Church of Rome to intervene in a dispute in which presbyters of Corinth had been deposed. Clement recalls that the Apostles, knowing that there would be strife over the office of bishop, "appointed" bishops and deacons, "and afterwards gave instructions that, when they should fall asleep, other approved men should succeed them in their ministry" (1 Clement 42:4-44:2). It is considered the oldest affirmation of the principle of apostolic succession.

One of the fullest testimonies, still in the second century, is that of Saint Irenaeus of Lyon, a disciple of Polycarp of Smyrna (who in turn had been a disciple of the Apostle John). Around the year 180 — the work «Against Heresies» is dated between 174 and 189, precisely because its list of bishops of Rome includes Eleutherius, then still living — Irenaeus presents, in Book III, chap. 3, a named and continuous list of the bishops of Rome: Peter and Paul, Linus, Anacletus, Clement, Evaristus, Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and finally Eleutherius, who "now, in the twelfth place from the Apostles, holds the inheritance of the episcopate". The purpose is polemical: to refute the Gnostics, showing that the apostolic faith could be traced publicly through this succession, unlike the secret traditions that the heretics claimed to possess.

Irenaeus calls the Church of Rome "the greatest, the oldest, and universally known, founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious Apostles, Peter and Paul", and writes that "it is necessary that every Church agree with this Church because of its more eminent origin" (the Latin expression is potiorem principalitatem, "stronger authority/primacy"). The same concern with the list of the first Roman bishops appears in Hegesippus, a second-century author who lived in Rome and whose testimony was transmitted by Eusebius of Caesarea (Ecclesiastical History IV, 11), who also records the tradition of the Roman episcopal succession from Peter. It is, therefore, testimony already from the second century to a role of reference attributed to the Roman see — although the exact scope of this primacy is still a matter of debate among historians and among the Christian traditions themselves.

The genuinely debated historical question is therefore not whether there was episcopal succession from early on — this is well documented by Clement, Ignatius of Antioch, Irenaeus and the tradition recorded by Eusebius — but the precise scope of the authority that this succession conferred on the bishop of Rome in particular. This point was developed doctrinally over the centuries and culminated in the definition of the First Vatican Council (1870). The dogmatic constitution «Pastor aeternus», promulgated by Pius IX on July 18, 1870, defines four doctrines: the apostolic primacy conferred on Peter, the perpetuity of this primacy in the Roman pontiffs, the papal primacy as supremacy, and the infallibility of the Pope when he speaks ex cathedra — that is, when, by virtue of his supreme apostolic authority, he defines doctrine of faith or morals, such definitions being "irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church". The final vote was 533 in favor and only 2 against, with about 60 bishops of the minority having left Rome so as not to take part in the approval; the two votes against were those of Bishops Aloisio Riccio and Edward Fitzgerald. Distinguishing the well-attested fact of early episcopal succession from the later development of papal doctrine is what makes the historical dialogue more precise.

itens.titulo: How does the Church today assess the medieval Crusades?
itens.resumo: The popes have publicly asked forgiveness for specific episodes of the Crusades — such as the sack of Constantinople in 1204 — and the current magisterium recognizes in them both religious motivations and grave abuses, without treating them as a morally uniform whole.
itens.corpo:
The Crusades were a series of military campaigns called by the Latin Church between 1095 and 1291. The starting point is the sermon of Pope Urban II (r. 1088-1099) at the Council of Clermont in November 1095 — the most frequently cited date is November 27 — which called on Christians to come to the aid of the East and to recover the Holy Places. The request had earlier roots: the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos had already asked the West for military support in 1095, at the Council of Piacenza, in the face of the expansion of the Seljuk Turks in Anatolia. Historians usually distinguish eight major expeditions in the traditional period (1095-1291), although the number varies according to the criterion adopted. The objectives were heterogeneous: to retake Jerusalem and the Holy Sepulchre, to answer Byzantium's appeals for help, to protect pilgrims, and to defend Christian territories. The First Crusade saw episodes such as the People's Crusade, led by Peter the Hermit, and ended with the capture of Jerusalem in 1099. It was the Second Vatican Council itself, in the declaration Nostra Aetate (1965), that, in recalling the common patrimony with Muslims, urged the Church to look upon them with esteem, and to face honestly the conflicts and hostilities of the past.

The contemporary Catholic Church does not treat the Crusades as a morally uniform whole. It recognizes in them genuine religious motivations and, at the same time, grave abuses incompatible with the Gospel. The most frequently cited episode is that of the Fourth Crusade (1202-1204), called by Pope Innocent III (r. 1198-1216) with the declared aim of retaking Jerusalem, lost in 1187. Because of financial difficulties — the crusaders could not pay the 85,000 silver marks the Venetians demanded for 240 ships — and because of Venice's commercial ambitions, the expedition was first diverted to Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, a Christian city held by the Hungarians, which was sacked in November 1202; Innocent III promptly excommunicated the crusaders and the Venetians, although the excommunication was later lifted for the crusaders. In April 1204 — the usual date is April 12 — the expedition sacked Constantinople, a Christian and allied city, deepening the schism between East and West. Many icons, relics, and works of art were carried off. Voices within the Church itself were already criticizing these excesses at the time.

The recent magisterium has begun to speak explicitly about specific episodes. The bull Incarnationis Mysterium (November 29, 1998), which proclaimed the Great Jubilee of the Year 2000, included among the signs of the Holy Year the "purification of memory," asking everyone for an act of courage and humility in recognizing "the wrongs done by those who have borne or bear the name of Christian." On March 12, 2000, on the so-called "Day of Pardon" of the Jubilee, John Paul II presided in Saint Peter's Basilica over a penitential celebration in which he asked forgiveness "for the divisions which have occurred among Christians" and "for the use of violence that some have committed in the service of truth."

The most specific gesture came on May 4, 2001, when John Paul II, on a visit to Athens, recalled before the Orthodox Archbishop Christodoulos — in a speech delivered at the Areopagus — the "disastrous sack of the imperial city of Constantinople" and stated that it was tragic that the assailants, who had set out to secure free access for Christians to the Holy Land, "turned against their own brothers in the faith," adding that the fact that they were Latin Christians filled Catholics with deep regret and asking: how can we not see there the "mysterium iniquitatis" at work in the human heart? On the same occasion, the Joint Declaration with Christodoulos condemned "every recourse to violence, proselytism and fanaticism, in the name of religion." In April 2004, on the eighth centenary of the sack, Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew I officially welcomed that request for forgiveness, acknowledging that a crime had been committed in the city eight hundred years earlier.

This does not mean that the Church today condemns the Crusades as a whole, nor that it justifies them without reservation: the current Catholic position combines the acknowledgment of sin and violence with historical analysis of intentions and contexts, distinguishing wars that could have defensive justifications from abuses of disproportionate violence.

itens.titulo: Did the Inquisition kill millions of people, as common sense suggests?
itens.resumo: Since the Archive of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith was opened to free consultation in January 1998, studies based on the trial records themselves have radically revised downward the numbers of the "black legend": the executions of the Spanish Inquisition were a few thousand, not millions.
itens.corpo:
The popular image of the Inquisition as a machine of mass extermination — with numbers in the millions — was largely shaped by the so-called "black legend," propaganda produced above all by Spain's rival powers and by Protestant authors from the sixteenth century onward, amid political and religious disputes. A landmark of this current was the calculation of the Spaniard Juan Antonio Llorente who, in 1817, a former secretary of the Holy Office itself, arrived at figures now considered absurdly inflated (tens of thousands condemned to death, of which about nine thousand under Torquemada alone), regarded by current historiography as untenable.

Modern historical research has reversed these numbers on the basis of the archived trial records themselves. A decisive step was the opening, in January 1998, of the Archive of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (the former Holy Office), made official in a ceremony presided over by the then prefect of the dicastery, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, at the National Academy of the Lincei in Rome, allowing historians to consult the collection freely. In the same year, an international historical symposium on the Inquisition organized by Agostino Borromeo was held at the Vatican, from October 29 to 31, 1998, and its proceedings were published in 2003 by the Vatican Apostolic Library (Studi e Testi, vol. 417). In 2000, the assessment of this work was presented to John Paul II, who again acknowledged the "dramas connected with the Inquisition" and described the Inquisition as a form of "counter-witness" and a "method of intolerance and violence in the service of the truth that disfigures the face of the Church."

The revised numbers are much smaller than those popularly circulated. The British historian Henry Kamen, one of the greatest authorities on the subject, working from archives and about 44,000 trials, arrived at an estimate of at most about three thousand executions over the entire history of the Spanish tribunal (1478-1834), noting that contemporary civil courts applied the death penalty in a similar or greater proportion — citing, for example, that the courts of the Low Countries executed many more heretics in the same period than the Inquisition did. Borromeo, for his part, in a study presented at the symposium, indicated that of the roughly 125,000 trials of the Spanish Inquisition, about 1% ended in execution; in absolute numbers, of the 44,674 trials between 1540 and 1700, only 1.8% received the death penalty, and about 1.7% of those were executions "in effigy" (of contumacious or already deceased defendants). Overall, fewer than half of the accused were convicted, and most penalties were light — penances, fines, exile. The bloodiest period was the earliest: under the first Inquisitor General, Tomás de Torquemada (1483-1498), it is now estimated that there were between 1,200 and 2,000 executions, mostly of converted Jews (conversos), far below the tens of thousands historically propagated.

None of this makes the Inquisition an institution without grave problems. The use of torture in interrogations (regulated and limited, but real), denunciation, and the very existence of ecclesiastical tribunals endowed with civil coercive power are today recognized as incompatible with the religious freedom taught by the Second Vatican Council, above all in the declaration "Dignitatis Humanae" (1965). In 2000, the document "Memory and Reconciliation: The Church and the Faults of the Past," of the International Theological Commission (a study that began at the request of then-Cardinal Ratzinger in view of the Jubilee, approved in specific form in 1999 and published dated March 7, 2000), dealt precisely with how the Church should critically assess episodes such as this without falling into exaggeration or denial.

The conclusion that imposes itself is twofold: to reject both the black legend that inflates the figures to millions and any attempt to minimize the real suffering of the victims. As Borromeo himself observed, historians today "no longer use this subject to defend or attack the Church"; the opened archives allow a documented judgment, and it is from this — not from the propaganda of either side — that the Church seeks to proceed.

itens.titulo: Can married men be ordained deacons in the Catholic Church?
itens.resumo: Since 1967, the Latin Church has restored the permanent diaconate, open also to married men of mature age — a discipline distinct from that required for the presbyterate, which remains tied to celibacy.
itens.corpo:
It is common to assume that every ordination in the Latin Church requires celibacy, which causes surprise at the presence of married permanent deacons in parishes. The explanation lies in a distinction that the Second Vatican Council made possible. The Dogmatic Constitution «Lumen Gentium», promulgated by Paul VI on November 21, 1964 (approved by the assembled bishops by a vote of 2,151 to 5), provides in no. 29 that, since the diaconal duties necessary to the life of the Church are difficult to fulfill in many regions under the discipline currently in force, «the diaconate can in the future be restored as a proper and permanent rank of the hierarchy». The same number provides that, with the consent of the Roman Pontiff, this diaconate may be conferred «on men of more mature age, even on those living in the married state», while for the young men admitted, «the law of celibacy must remain intact». The historical context is worth noting: the diaconate had existed as a stable state in the early centuries (there were bishops and even popes who had been deacons), but in the medieval Latin Church it ended up reduced to a transitional stage on the way to the presbyterate — it was precisely this situation that the Council wished to reverse.

The regulation came with Paul VI's apostolic letter «Sacrum Diaconatus Ordinem», issued motu proprio on June 18, 1967, which restored the permanent diaconate in the Latin Church. The document specifies that married men are to be promoted to the diaconate only if, after many years of married life, they have shown that they govern their own household well and have a wife and children who live an exemplary Christian life (no. 13); and that men of mature age, whether celibate or married, may be called, with married men not being admitted «unless there is certainty not only of the wife's consent, but also of her irreproachable Christian life» (no. 11). The same document determines that a married deacon who becomes a widower may not contract a new marriage (no. 16). The following year, the Apostolic Constitution «Pontificalis Romani Recognitio» (June 17, 1968) approved the new rite of ordination of the deacon, the priest and the bishop.

A second normative stage came with Paul VI's apostolic letter «Ad Pascendum», of August 15, 1972, which established complementary norms on the diaconate, including the specific rite of admission of candidates and details on the ministry and life of married deacons. Later, in 1998, the Holy See published the «Basic Norms for the Formation of Permanent Deacons», which defined service as the axis of diaconal spirituality and required of married deacons, like the others, an intense life of prayer and the «unity of life» among ministry, family and work.

In practice, the permanent deacon exercises ministries such as the proclamation of the Gospel, preaching, the administration of Baptism, assisting at Marriage in the name of the Church, the distribution of Communion and works of charity, without access to the presbyterate. A married deacon who becomes a widower may not contract a new marriage (cf. «Sacrum Diaconatus Ordinem», no. 16), and the discipline of celibacy remains the general rule for those ordained while already unmarried, whether as young permanent deacons or as priests. The distinction, therefore, is not between being married or not, but between the diaconate — which admits married men of mature age — and the presbyterate, for which the Latin Church maintains the discipline of celibacy.

itens.titulo: Does "Outside the Church There Is No Salvation" Mean That Only Practicing Catholics Will Be Saved?
itens.resumo: The formula "extra Ecclesiam nulla salus" affirms that all salvation comes from Christ through the Church, not that those who have never known her are automatically condemned; condemnation falls upon conscious and culpable rejection.
itens.corpo:
The Latin formula "extra Ecclesiam nulla salus" (outside the Church there is no salvation) is very ancient. Its form closest to the classical text appears in the letter of Saint Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage (martyred in 258), addressed to Jubaianus on the validity of baptism given by heretics — in the Cyprianic correspondence, Epistle 72 (or 73, depending on the collection): "Salus extra ecclesiam non est" ("there is no salvation outside the Church"). The original context was therefore a dispute over who could validly confer baptism, and not a verdict on the pagans who had never heard of the Gospel. The idea was taken up by other Fathers, such as Firmilian, and by the patristic tradition, which saw the Church as Noah's ark — only within it would there be salvation.

The strongest and most frequently cited formulation in the Western magisterium is the bull Unam Sanctam of Pope Boniface VIII, dated November 18, 1302, written in the midst of a serious conflict with King Philip IV the Fair of France. The document states that "outside this one Church there is no salvation nor remission of sins," and concludes by declaring "that it is absolutely necessary for the salvation of every human creature to be subject to the Roman Pontiff." The historian Brian Tierney considers it "probably the most famous document" on the relations between Church and State in medieval Europe; the original has been lost, and its text is known through the registers of Boniface VIII in the Vatican Archives.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church itself (nos. 846-848) distinguishes the positive sense of the formula from its exclusive sense. Positively, it means that all salvation comes from Christ the Head through the Church, his Body — Christ is the only mediator, and the Church is the visible and necessary instrument of this plan, not one among several equivalent paths. Negatively, the formula condemns those who, "knowing that the Catholic Church was founded as necessary by God through Jesus Christ, would refuse either to enter her or to remain in her." The Dogmatic Constitution Lumen Gentium of the Second Vatican Council (1964), in treating in its no. 14 of those who are not saved, speaks explicitly of those who, "knowing that the Catholic Church was founded as necessary by God through Christ, would refuse to enter or to remain in it" — that is, culpable rejection, not ignorance. No. 16 of the same constitution, and the Declaration Nostra Aetate (1965), extend the hope of salvation to those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel and the Church, but seek God with a sincere heart.

The limits of this doctrine were tested in the twentieth century in the case of the Jesuit Leonard Feeney, of Boston College, who defended a rigid reading: he denied the value of baptism of blood and baptism of desire and maintained that non-Catholics would be damned. On August 8, 1949, the Congregation of the Holy Office sent to the Archbishop of Boston, Archbishop Richard Cushing, a letter — approved by Pius XII on July 28 of that year — clarifying that, for eternal salvation, it is not always required that a person be actually incorporated into the Church as a member, but it is enough to belong to her "at least in desire and longing"; and that, where there is invincible ignorance, God accepts even an implicit desire. Feeney refused to submit, was excommunicated in 1953, and was reconciled with the Church in 1972, without ever having publicly retracted his theses. The formula, therefore, has never been understood by the Church as an assertion that only practicing Catholics are saved.

itens.titulo: Why Does the Catholic Bible Have Seven More Books Than the Bible Used by Most Protestants?
itens.resumo: The seven deuterocanonical books were in the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament used by the first Christians; they were reaffirmed by councils of the fourth century and by Florence (1442), and solemnly confirmed by the Council of Trent in 1546.
itens.corpo:
The question is usually framed the opposite way from what history suggests: it is not so much that the Catholic Church "added" books, but that the Protestant reformers of the sixteenth century, following the Palestinian Jewish canon, began to set aside — and ended up excluding from Protestant Bibles — seven books that Christians had been reading for centuries: Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), and Baruch, as well as passages added to Esther and Daniel. These books were part of the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament used by Greek-speaking Jews and by the first Christians, and frequently cited by the New Testament itself. The terminological confusion is old: Catholics call them "deuterocanonical" (from the Greek, "of the second canon") and Protestants call them "apocrypha."

These books already appeared in ancient canonical lists. The so-called Gelasian Decree (Decretum Gelasianum de libris recipiendis et non recipiendis), traditionally attributed to Pope Gelasius I (492-496), includes in its second chapter a complete catalog of the Scriptures; it is now considered that this list partly reflects a Roman canon linked to Pope Damasus I and the Council of Rome of 382, even though the text received its final form around 519-553, the work of an anonymous author. Equivalent lists were adopted by the North African councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397), under the strong influence of Saint Augustine. Later, the Council of Florence (1442), in the bull Cantate Domino, once again enumerated the canonical books.

In the sixteenth century, the question was reopened with the advance of Renaissance philology. As early as 1520, Andreas Bodenstein von Karlstadt, in the booklet De canonicis Scripturis libellus (Wittenberg), described the seven books as "apocrypha." Martin Luther, following the criterion of the "veritas hebraica" that he attributed to Saint Jerome, did not remove them in his German translation of the Bible of 1534 (Biblia, das ist die gantze Heilige Schrift deutsch), but placed them at the end of the volume under the title "Apokrypha," with the qualification: "Apokrypha, das sind Bücher, so nicht der heiligen Schrift gleich gehalten, und doch nützlich und gut zu lesen sind" ("Apocrypha, that is, books not equated with Sacred Scripture, but useful and good to read"). It is worth noting that Saint Jerome, in the prologue to the books of Samuel and Kings — the so-called Prologus Galeatus — did in fact distinguish the books outside the Hebrew canon, although in practice he treated some of them almost as canonical; the Western Church, however, did not adopt his strict classification.

In the face of Protestant challenge, the Council of Trent, in its fourth session (April 8, 1546), solemnly defined the canon, listing the books "entire with all their parts" and pronouncing an anathema on anyone who did not receive them — explicitly mentioning, among others, "Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Baruch, two books of Maccabees." The canon was fixed at 73 books: 46 in the Old Testament and 27 in the New. It should be remembered that the elimination of the deuterocanonical books from Protestant Bibles was not immediate: in 1618-1619, some Calvinists at the Synod of Dort proposed their suppression, and only on May 3, 1826 did the British Bible Society decide that these writings should no longer be circulated together with Sacred Scripture.

itens.titulo: Can a Catholic Believe in Reincarnation?
itens.resumo: The Catechism explicitly states that "there is no 'reincarnation' after death"; each person lives only one earthly life, followed by judgment — a doctrine already defended against the preexistence of souls since the sixth century.
itens.corpo:
The idea of reincarnation — the soul migrating, after death, into a new body in a sequence of successive lives — is common to various religious traditions and Eastern philosophies and today has a considerable presence in Western culture, including among people who call themselves Christians. The Catholic Church explicitly rejects this possibility. The Catechism states, in no. 1013: "There is no 'reincarnation' after death." More fully: "Death is the end of man's earthly pilgrimage... When 'the single course of our earthly life' is completed, we shall not return to other earthly lives. 'It is appointed for men to die once' (Heb 9:27). There is no 'reincarnation' after death." The biblical foundation is the Letter to the Hebrews, which sets out the uniqueness and unrepeatability of each person's earthly life, followed by judgment — and which presents Christ, by contrast, as the one who offered himself "once for all" (Heb 9:26-28; 10:10).

This rejection has roots in the first centuries. Origen of Alexandria (c. 185-253/254), in works such as De Principiis (Peri Archon) and Contra Celsum, upheld the preexistence of souls and their fall into bodies — a thesis that served as the speculative basis for the idea of previous lives — as well as apokatastasis, the final restoration of all creatures, including the demons. In 543, the Emperor Justinian I condemned these doctrines by decree, and the Second Council of Constantinople (553) — the Fifth Ecumenical Council — included among its documents fifteen anathemas against Origen, the first of which states: "If anyone asserts the fabled preexistence of souls, and the monstrous restoration which follows from it, let him be anathema." The ninth of these anathemas specifically condemns apokatastasis: "If anyone says or thinks that the punishment of the wicked and of the demons will be temporary and will have an end at some time, that is, that there will be a restoration of the demons or of wicked men, let him be anathema." The council met in Constantinople from May 5 to June 2, 553, convened by Justinian I and presided over by Patriarch Eutychius of Constantinople; it had about 166 bishops, of whom only sixteen were Western (from the provinces of Africa Proconsularis and Illyricum). It is the oldest formal condemnation of a doctrine that underlay the idea of rebirths.

In the same vein, Fathers of the West had already refuted, in the fourth and fifth centuries, forms of the transmigration of souls then in circulation. Saint Augustine devoted part of The City of God (begun in 413 and completed in 426, in 22 books, after thirteen years of work) to affirming that God created man only once in time and to denying the Platonic doctrine of recollection and metempsychosis, defending in its place the Christian doctrine of the resurrection of the body; in books XI and XII, in treating the origin of the soul and of time, he rejects the idea of souls that "remember" previous lives. Saint Jerome and Saint Ambrose also opposed the preexistence of souls.

The alternative that the Catholic faith proposes to reincarnation is not extinction, but the resurrection of the flesh: not a new earthly life repeated in another body, but definitive life, united forever to God or separated from him, according to each person's particular judgment at the end of the one earthly existence. The Catechism places this affirmation in a broader pastoral context: it exhorts the faithful to prepare for the hour of death and warns against seeking consolation in supposed spiritist revelations, presented as a deception that diverts man from the task of seeking salvation.

itens.titulo: How can the Church say that the Pope is infallible if several popes led morally scandalous lives?
itens.resumo: Infallibility and impeccability are distinct concepts: the dogma defined at Vatican I (1870) guarantees immunity from error only in solemn ex cathedra definitions of faith and morals, not the absence of personal sin nor the correctness of every papal teaching.
itens.corpo:
The objection usually confuses two distinct theological concepts: infallibility and impeccability. Impeccability would be the incapacity to sin — something the Church has never attributed to any pope. Infallibility, solemnly defined by the First Vatican Council in the dogmatic constitution "Pastor Aeternus," promulgated by Pius IX on July 18, 1870, is the guarantee, given by the assistance of the Holy Spirit, that the pope does not err when he defines solemnly, "ex cathedra" — that is, exercising his office as shepherd and teacher of all Christians —, a doctrine of faith or morals to be held by the whole Church. It is neither a permanent charism nor an unlimited power: the council itself clarified that the Holy Spirit was promised to the successors of Peter not so that they might preach new doctrine, but so that they might guard and faithfully expound the deposit of faith. For this reason the definition was accompanied by intense debate: in the vote of July 13, 1870, of the 601 council fathers present, 451 voted "placet," 88 voted "non placet," and 62 accepted with reservations ("placet iuxta modum"); in the final public session on July 18, with the minority already largely withdrawn from Rome, 433 voted "placet" and only two bishops — Aloisio Riccio of Cajazzo and Edward Fitzgerald of Little Rock — voted "non placet," and both soon afterward adhered to the definition. The council was furthermore interrupted a few months later, in September 1870, by the capture of Rome by the Kingdom of Italy and the end of the Papal States.

It should be noted that a solemn ex cathedra definition is something extremely rare in history. The two cases that are practically undisputed among theologians are the bull "Ineffabilis Deus" (1854) of Pius IX, which defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, and the constitution "Munificentissimus Deus" (1950) of Pius XII, on the Assumption of Mary. All the rest of ordinary papal teaching does not automatically enjoy this specific guarantee, although it demands respect and religious assent.

Cases such as that of Pope Alexander VI (1492–1503) illustrate precisely this distinction. Born Rodrigo Borgia, of a Valencian family, he was elected on August 11, 1492, and his pontificate — recognized by Catholic historiography itself as one of the most scandalous — was marked by open nepotism (such as the promotion of his children Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia to positions of power), by children born outside of celibacy, and by deep immersion in the political and military intrigues of Renaissance Italy. However grave his personal conduct was, he never went so far as to define any heretical doctrine as a dogma of faith in the name of the whole Church — which is the only condition with which infallibility is concerned.

The most delicate case in history is not that of a sinful pope, but of a pope accused of heresy. Honorius I (625–638), little versed in the subtleties of Greek theology, replied in a private letter to Patriarch Sergius of Constantinople approving a formula that spoke of a single will in Christ, thus favoring Monothelitism. The Sixth Ecumenical Council, gathered in Constantinople between 680 and 681 and ratified by the representatives of Pope Agatho, condemned Monothelitism and included Honorius among those anathematized; his successor Leo II confirmed the condemnation, interpreting it, however, as negligence: Honorius "did not strive to keep this Apostolic Church pure in the doctrine of apostolic tradition, but permitted, by a profane betrayal, this immaculate Church to be defiled" (letter to Constantine IV, in Mansi, XI, 733). The current theological response is that Honorius's letter was an act of private ordinary magisterium, not an ex cathedra definition, and that the error lay precisely in his not having taught in continuity with the tradition received; for this reason he was included in the lists of anathematized heretics and in the papal oath of the "Liber diurnus" until the eleventh century.

The Catholic tradition reads the Church's persistence, despite the personal weakness — at times extreme — of some of her popes and even errors in non-defining acts, as a sign, and not a refutation, that her ultimate doctrinal unity does not depend on the personal holiness or the theological competence of each successor of Peter, but on Christ's promise to Peter (Lk 22:32) and to the Church (Mt 16:18). The distinction between the office and the person of its holder is therefore the key to the question: infallibility is a guarantee given to the office under strict conditions, not a certificate of virtue for its occupant.

itens.titulo: Why Is the Catholic Church Opposed to the Use of Artificial Contraceptive Methods?
itens.resumo: In the encyclical "Humanae Vitae" (July 25, 1968), Paul VI taught that artificial contraception improperly separates the unitive and procreative meanings of the conjugal act, rejecting the majority opinion of the study commission that he himself had enlarged.
itens.corpo:
On July 25, 1968, after a long and controversial process of consultation, Pope Paul VI published the encyclical "Humanae Vitae" (subtitle: "On the Regulation of Birth"), reaffirming the traditional teaching that the use of artificial contraceptive methods is morally unacceptable. The context was that of the sexual revolution and the spread of the contraceptive pill. In March 1963, John XXIII had created a Pontifical Commission for the Study of Population, Family and Birth; Paul VI confirmed and enlarged this commission, adding to it also married couples and scholars from various disciplines ("Humanae Vitae," no. 5), precisely in order to offer the Magisterium the elements needed for a response to the new questions connected with married life.

The internal result of the commission was, however, divided and deeply controversial. In 1966, the majority report, known as the "Draft of the Document Concerning Responsible Parenthood" and later leaked to the press, proposed that artificial contraception was not intrinsically evil and that couples could decide for themselves which methods to use; according to reports, this opinion was approved by 64 of the 69 voting members. A minority report, associated with figures such as Cardinal Alfredo Ottaviani and Bishop Carlo Colombo, defended the continuity of the doctrine. Paul VI also consulted the synod fathers in October 1967, although only about 12% of them responded, and the majority of those responses favored the lawfulness of artificial methods. The final decision, therefore, was made against the weight of the opinions consulted, which explains a good part of the later controversy; the definitive text was approved on July 8, 1968, and presented to the press on July 29 of that year.

The central argument of "Humanae Vitae" is not merely disciplinary but anthropological. According to Catholic doctrine, the conjugal act has, inseparably, a twofold meaning, unitive (the mutual gift of the spouses) and procreative (openness to the possible generation of new life), and artificially separating these two meanings, by deliberately preventing the fruitfulness of an act that is being performed, would distort the proper language of conjugal sexuality. Hence the formula of no. 11: "each and every marriage act must remain open to the transmission of life." The Church distinguishes this position from the use of natural methods of regulating fertility (such as methods of observing the cycle), which do not artificially prevent the fruitfulness of the act, but choose, for just reasons, the periods in which it is performed; and the document expressly rejects sterilization and abortion. Paul VI also warned, in the text, of the consequences he foresaw: the facilitation of conjugal infidelity, the degradation of women treated as objects, and the risk that states might impose birth control policies.

The reaction was one of the most contentious in the recent history of the papal magisterium. On the very day of the presentation, theologians from the Catholic University of America, among them Father Charles Curran, drafted a "Statement of Dissent"; numerous theologians, bishops and entire episcopal conferences expressed reservations, and there was a significant drop in religious practice in several countries. Some episcopal conferences, such as that of Canada, sought to interpret the document pastorally, with emphasis on the formation of conscience. The teaching was reiterated by John Paul II in the apostolic exhortation "Familiaris Consortio" (November 22, 1981), which reaffirmed the prohibition of contraception and described spouses who use it as "arbiters" of the divine plan who alter the value of the total gift of self (no. 32), and it remains the Church's doctrinal frame of reference, deepened in later documents and reaffirmed in the Catechism (nos. 2366-2372).
